hints: Remember what complete combustion in excess oxygen always makes for a hydrocarbon, think carbon dioxide and water only.
Start with the formula of hexane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$, so 1 mole must give 6 moles of $\text{CO}_2$ from the 6 carbons.
Now balance the 14 hydrogens to find the moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, then add the two product amounts together.
walkthrough:
**Recall the products of complete combustion**

A hydrocarbon burning in excess oxygen gives only carbon dioxide and water. No carbon monoxide or carbon is formed here.

General idea:
$$\text{hydrocarbon} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Write the balanced equation for hexane**

Hexane is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$. All 6 carbons become $\text{CO}_2$, so we get 6 moles. All 14 hydrogens become $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so we need 7 moles.

Balanced equation:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14} + \tfrac{19}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2 + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Count total moles of products**

Products are only what is on the right hand side. Do not include the excess oxygen, it is a reactant.

Total calculation:
$$\text{moles products} = 6 + 7 = 13$$

options.A: 11 is too low. It often comes from miscounting the water molecules, for example using 5 moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ instead of balancing the 14 H atoms correctly to 7 moles.
options.B: 12 is incorrect. It usually comes from getting 6 moles of $\text{CO}_2$ correct but only 6 moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, forgetting that $\text{H}_{14}$ needs 7 waters to balance.
options.C: 13 is correct. From $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14} + \tfrac{19}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2 + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$, 1 mole of hexane gives 6 moles of carbon dioxide plus 7 moles of water, giving 13 moles of products in total.
options.D: 14 is too high. It often comes from counting the hexane itself or the oxygen as a product, or from rounding the water up to 8 moles instead of the correct balanced value of 7.
